$comment: Which of two sealed configs to keep, read by tests/main/vaultorder.test.ts and the Android SharedCorpusTest. Both devices have to answer this identically or they trade vaults forever, or worse, one of them quietly rolls the other back.
$cases: `current` is what this device holds — null for a device with no vault yet. `currentIsPlaceholder` says that config was made automatically rather than chosen, and defaults to false. `adopt` is whether the incoming one replaces it.

cases.name: a device with no config takes whatever it is offered

cases.$comment: Rollback protection: an older vault may carry a password somebody already has, and a later timestamp on it proves nothing.
cases.name: an older version loses however recently it was sealed

cases.$comment: Both devices edited while unable to see each other. Without this they each refuse the other as 'not newer' and stay apart until somebody edits again.
cases.name: at the same version, the later edit wins
and the earlier one does not

cases.$comment: As far as anything here can tell this is the same config. Adopting would have two devices swapping identical vaults for as long as both were running.
cases.name: a tie on both is not a reason to do anything
a timestamp we cannot compare settles nothing

cases.$comment: A phone makes itself a config on first launch so that adding a server is not gated on owning a desktop. That config is a placeholder: nobody chose it, nothing is in it, and it is sealed with a random key rather than a passphrase. Before this case it outranked the desktop's real config on the timestamp tiebreak — because a phone is always set up after the desktop it pairs to — and pairing then succeeded while quietly sharing nothing.
cases.name: a config nobody chose yields to one somebody did

cases.$comment: Even an older one. There is nothing in a placeholder to roll back.
cases.name: even an older config, since a placeholder holds nothing to lose

cases.$comment: Whether the other device holds a placeholder is not asked and could not be trusted if it were: the envelope's visible fields are authenticated, so adding a claim there would mean a format change, and a claim from a peer is the wrong thing to weigh anyway. A device that holds a placeholder does not offer it — see the vault-offer gate — so this direction never arises on the wire.
cases.name: the flag describes only the device asking, never the one offering
